item: A host name with spaces is refused before the SSRF guard looks it up, and no guard sentence begins with a host (R622)
refs: R622 R614 R616 R620 PR pending
summary: R622 (the merge steward's security read, coordinator queue item 47). BEFORE: a redirect hop handed urlparse(nxt).hostname to EthicalFetcher._guard_target before the next turn of the loop ran _refuse_parser_mismatch on it, and fetch(), declared_sitemaps(), preflight._check_one and feed_preflight._check_host_robots handed theirs to the guard with no such check. urlparse keeps spaces and lower-cases, so a Location or a source can name the host 'network kill switch is active -- collection stopped by operator' in any case, and the guard's resolve-time sentence '<host> resolves to a non-public address (...)' began with it. MEASURED: glibc 2.39 refuses a name holding a space or a tab before any DNS packet (strace), so on this machine the lookup failed as 'cannot resolve host ...' (fixed words, read as dns). With a resolver that answers such a name with a non-public address (simulated under the socket guard), the initial-target paths and a hop whose connect scope stood down (a proxy given by name, OO_SSRF_CONNECT_GUARD=0) wrote the switch's whole sentence first: is_kill_switch_refusal said yes, the robots read's refused_by_name re-raised it uncached (the host was never backed off), the pipeline and both preflights read skipped_offline, and the health count with a Stop pressed after the probe counted it refused_by_kill_switch. With the connect scope live, ssrf_guard.check_resolution's own sentence (fixed words) came first. R622 ships the fix as defence in depth either way. NOW: on every hop _refuse_parser_mismatch(nxt) runs BEFORE the guard, and the Location is also read with a tab, CR or LF shown as a space, because urljoin deletes them on a same-scheme hop (a bracketed host that is then unreadable is refused, never a ValueError); fetch(), declared_sitemaps() and both preflights call _refuse_parser_mismatch before the guard; _guard_target itself refuses a host holding a backslash, whitespace or a control character before any lookup, in fixed words, for a caller that does not check first; its resolve-time sentence now begins "refusing to fetch '<host>': it resolves". FROM THE INDEPENDENT READ, two bare ValueErrors that escaped the fetch (the robots read never backed the host off, and ingest_url did not catch them): a Location urlsplit cannot read (an unclosed IPv6 bracket), which requests itself parses to build Response.next even with allow_redirects=False, is now FetchFailed 'redirect to a URL that cannot be read', from the session's get and from the fetcher's own urljoin; and a name socket.getaddrinfo cannot IDNA-encode (an empty label, a label over 63 characters) is now FetchFailed 'cannot resolve host ...: the name cannot be encoded for a lookup', raised outside the handler so record_text does not write it as the UnicodeError's fixed record. TESTS: tests/test_host_whitespace_r622.py, 74 (56 of the first 63 fail on 8e1f59a28, the 7 controls pass), a real fetcher through a loopback proxy given by name with only the resolver stood in; tests/test_refusal_sentence.py's IPvFuture case pinned the old order and now expects the guard's fixed refusal. Fifteen mutants (the hop's order put back; each of the hop's two reads, its ValueError translation, the four callers' checks and the guard's own check removed; the host-first sentence put back; for the read's fold, each of the two ValueError catches and the UnicodeError catch removed, and each raised inside its handler): none survived. NOT CHANGED: src/safety/fetcher.py (it never calls _guard_target, and refuse_unlisted_host already runs _refuse_parser_mismatch first); sitemap.py's report.errors lines that begin with a sitemap URL (no reader classifies them); the 'cannot resolve host' and ssrf_guard sentences (fixed words first). Release-notes line: «A redirect or a source whose host name holds spaces, a backslash or control characters is now refused before any lookup, so a site can no longer make its own failure look like the operator's Stop. A redirect to an address that cannot be read now counts as that site's own failure. (R622)»
